label: Won't Fix
summary: Unregistered users can see "public" messages from a closed wiki via notifications from a different wiki
description:
If a wiki is closed to unregistered users by setting the black checkbox "Prevent unregistered users from viewing pages", and another wiki has a public page with a notification stream which also shows events from that wiki, then anonymous users can see the "publicMessages" (i.e. send to all users of that wiki) in that notifications. This can be fixed by explicitly denying unregistered users the "view"-right wiki wide (with that red stop sign).

To reproduce, grab a jetty-hsql test instance, fire it up and:

* log in as admin
* create a subwiki
* go to the wiki administration of that subwiki
* in the "Right" section set the black checkbox to prevent unregistered users viewing pages in the wiki
* in "Message Stream" activate the message stream of that wiki
* go to the dashboard of that wiki and create a message which is visible to "everyone"
* reload the subwiki dashboard to see the that the message has been posted
* go back to the main wiki and visit the dashboard there to check the message is there
* log out of the main wiki
* visit the dashboard as unregistered user

Expected: message should not be show to the unregistered user
Actual: unregistered user see the message in the notification stream in the dashboard

If the "view" right is denied to unregistered users wiki-wide in the subwiki, the message is not longer shown.

One can try the same from another subwiki by setting the "wikis" parameter of the notification macro. In that case the message will not be shown to users registered in the other wiki, but to unregistered users if the page with the notifications is visible to them.

Not sure if it is really a bug, as "Prevent unregistered users from viewing pages" does not talk about messages, but I guess it will be at least unexpected.

comments.author: Simon Urli
comments.body: I don't see that as a bug: you explicitely send a message to "everyone" so for me it also includes non-registered users.

comments.author: Clemens Robbenhaar
comments.body:
Admittedly it depends what you think "everyone" is. I think that users in a closed wiki will feel that only registered users in their wiki are "everyone". But that is just my opinion.

If you think that this behavior is not a bug, just close it as "Invalid".

comments.author: Simon Urli
comments.body:
bq.  I think that users in a closed wiki will feel that only registered users in their wiki are "everyone". But that is just my opinion.

You're right, I might have been a bit too fast in my first answer.
Now this is not an easy one to fix: we usually use the attached document reference of an event to define if it should be displayed or not, and it's obviously not possible for messages. 
We discussed a bit with [~tmortagne] about it, so I paste the discussion here:

{noformat}
Simon Urli
Thomas: I'm reading again https://jira.xwiki.org/browse/XWIKI-17154 and I'm wondering if we shouldn't actually implement a filter to not display notifications to guest users when they are coming from a close wiki. We generally don't have the problem since notifications are generally attached to documents, but as soon it's no longer the case we have rights issue for them. WDYT?

Thomas
One problem is that there is no clear criteria to define "a close wiki".
Even in a wiki where guests don't have view right at wiki level they usually have it in some pages like password reset for technical reasons for example.
and you might have given guest view right only on some spaces like the Main so it's hardly a criteria that works
Of course if you mean an optional filter than an admin can enable then sure but I doubt everyone will see this as enough (since no admin will ever think about that)

Simon Urli
what would be the criteria for notifications not attached to a document then? special

comments.author: Simon Urli
comments.body: I'm really wondering if we should not close it as a wontfix since Message Stream is not really supported anymore, but maybe we're not clear enough about that. Also for me, the easiest fix would be to be more clear that posting a message to "everyone" means "everyone in the farm" and not just in the wiki.

comments.author: Simon Urli
comments.body: It's been voted to deprecate and remove Message Stream from XS. See https://forum.xwiki.org/t/deprecate-and-remove-message-stream-from-xwiki-standard/14780/

comments.author: Simon Urli
comments.body: Reopening: we need to inform users that the feature is deprecated and using it could be dangerous because of vulnerabilities that won't be fixed. And we need an advisory for this.

label: Fixed
summary: Security access entries for guests aren't cached in the security cache
description:
Since fixing XWIKI-18508, access right checks for public access to the wiki aren't cached anymore. This could lead to slightly degraded performance.

The reason for this is that the cache now checks that for security access entries, the indicated user parent entry is actually a user entry but at the same time, loading this user entry fails for the guest user. The reason for this is that the DefaultSecurityEntryReader doesn't load any rules for the guest user and then insertion into the security cache fails because a main wiki entry with rules already exists.

summary: Some large documents cannot be exported to PDF anymore using new PDF Export
description:
*Steps to reproduce*
 # Create a large page with a lot of content, including tables (tested with an Office Imported Word document, for easy reproduction {_}please use the attached XAR{_})
 # Login as Admin
 # Go to Administer Wiki > Content > PDF Export and from Generator select "User Browser"
 # Go to the created page, click More Actions > Export > PDF > Export > Export (keeping the default Export Options)
 # Go to Administer Wiki > Content > PDF Export and from Generator select "Chrome Docker Container"
 # Go back to the created page, click More Actions > Export > PDF > Export > Export

 # Go to the created page, click More Actions > Export > PDF > Export > Export

*Expected results*

The page is exported to PDF.

*Actual results*

When using User Browser (Edge 116, Chrome 116 and Firefox 117), Docker Container and Remote Chrome, after a long waiting, the error message:
{code:java}
Failed to export as PDF: Timeout waiting for web page to be ready for print.{code}
is displayed.

Tested also by increasing Page Ready Timeout to 500, but, nevertheless, the PDF file is not exported.

The issue could not be reproduced on XWiki 14.10.15, where the PDF is exported without having to increase Page Ready Timeout (except when using User Browser on Firefox, where I got the same timeout error message and increased the Timeout to 500, but the PDF was generated earlier than the timeout limit).

The issue couldn't also be reproduced on XWiki 15.5.2, except for when using User Browser on Firefox 117, where although the Timeout was set to 500, the PDF seems to not be generated in the end (same Timeout error message).

It is to be mentioned that the page is exported to PDF using old PDF (FOP) export (also within a shorter time).

label: Fixed
summary: When saving a new version of an attachment, the store should make sure the content/archive stores do not change
description: It does not make any sense to change the store of an attachment when adding a new version, so the store should make sure it does not happen (i.e. make sure to reuse the content/archive store from an already stored attachment).

label: Fixed
summary: History navigation arrows are not perceived as links and lacking contrast
description:
We present arrows in the banner of the history when seeing a diff to allow browsing to another version. So we have big arrows to move to major versions and small arrows to move to minor versions. 
 !image-2023-08-30-10-10-21-906.png|thumbnail! 
Sadly those arrows are displayed in white on grey, making them almost invisible, and on top of it it's not clear at all that those are links, so users just don't know at all about this feature.

comments.author: Charpentier Lucas
comments.body:
Those are links since they navigate to a new page. However, they only allow to change URL parameters, which do not change the kind of content of the page drastically. This makes them fall under the umbrella term of action links.
Since those are action links, I propose we style them as buttons, just like the action menu items ( #tmEdit, #tmCreate, #tmMoreActions, ...).

This way, it will be more consistent and easier to understand for users, and all the regular button style rules will be applied to provide a proper contrast.

label: Fixed
summary: Default home page comes with velocity scripts
description:
Following XWIKI-20321, members of xwiki:XWiki.XWikiAllGroup don't get script rights by default on the main wiki.

While this gives great benefits in regards with security, it also creates a situation where standard users cannot edit a part of the default home page without having velocity errors, because the home page comes by default with two velocity scripts : 

* One for adding the xwiki version passed as a parameter to a documentation page on xwiki.org : https://github.com/xwiki/xwiki-platform/blob/b697f3c99270e837c134e7a66d202b18826f546f/xwiki-platform-distribution/xwiki-platform-distribution-flavor/xwiki-platform-distribution-flavor-common/src/main/resources/Main/WebHome.xml#L56C33-L56C33
* One for creating a URL to access the extension manager in XWiki Preferences : https://github.com/xwiki/xwiki-platform/blob/b697f3c99270e837c134e7a66d202b18826f546f/xwiki-platform-distribution/xwiki-platform-distribution-flavor/xwiki-platform-distribution-flavor-common/src/main/resources/Main/WebHome.xml#L64C5-L64C5

The second link can be replaced as {{[[Extension Manager>>XWiki.XWikiPreferences||queryString="editor=globaladmin&section=XWiki.Extensions"]]}} (taking advantage of the fact that the user will be redirected automatically to the admin action.

The first link is more difficult to modify ; currently I don't know how we use this version for our documentation on xwiki.org

The problem that this situation causes a bad experience for new users testing out XWiki without being necessarily the ones that have installed the XWiki instance (and thus being admins). The home page looks like a pretty normal page, and users get confused / don't understand why red messages appear once they change the first paragraph.

We could think of two options for this issue : 
* Either remove completely any velocity macro, so that the home page is editable again by users without scripting rights
* Or only grant edit rights on this page to XWikiAdminGroup by default, so that only admins can edit it.

label: Fixed
summary: A rollback does not trigger right protection
description:
Reproduction steps: 
  - On a fresh wiki with standard rights, login with Admin create a page Test and a user Foo
  - Administer page Test to forbid Delete right to Foo on the page only: the UI forces you to first grant the right and then deny it
  - History of the page should have 3 version for Test: original creation, grant of delete right and deny of delete right
  - Login with Foo, you should have edit right on Test with standard right scheme, go to history and tries to rollback to second version (which grant delete right)

Expected result:
  - the UI link should be available (because of edit right) but the action should either lead to an error and shouldn't do anything

Obtained result:
  - the link is working, the rollback is performed and Foo is now able to delete the page Test

This can also be done by deleting the current version from the history (which cause a rollback of the document to the previous version).

The root cause is that those two rollbacks causes ("rollback" and "current version delete from the history") are missing a call to XWiki#checkSavingDocument which is in charge of producing `UserUpdatingDocumentEvent` event which is what `RightsFilterListener` rely on.

description:
How to reproduce:
* go to the XWiki login form
* fill in credentials (wrong ones for highlighting this problem, but it does just the same for correct credentials)
* double click login button
** or click as many times as you want

Expected result:
* the authentication process is launched a single time, and the login button is disabled when the form has been sent and until an answer is received from the server

comments.author: Anca Luca
comments.body: This is particularly tricky if used with custom authenticators that _may_ create user profiles following how those authenticators handle parallel requests. The LDAP authenticator, for example, assumes that no double authentication request will be launched in parallel and thus this situation is problematic (see LDAP-135).

comments.author: Manuel Leduc
comments.body: Note that afaics this only reproduces on Chrome, and not on Firefox.

comments.author: Anca Luca
comments.body:
bq. Note that afaics this only reproduces on Chrome, and not on Firefox.

[~mleduc]: What would stop it from reproducing on Firefox? Is the login button disabled on Firefox after the first submit?
As far as I know http protocol does not have any way of "recalling" an http request once it's sent to the server and this "recalling" is the only thing that could stop the multiple processing on the server...

comments.author: Manuel Leduc
comments.body: [~lucaa] I did not dig deeper. Afaik it's a very standard form. What I can tell is that I smashed the submit button several times on both browsers and was only able to reproduce on chrome.

comments.author: Anca Luca
comments.body:
bq. What I can tell is that I smashed the submit button several times on both browsers and was only able to reproduce on chrome.

Especially since it's the most standard form, from the pov of the browser, it would indeed "abandon" a navigation to an URL if another navigation is started in the mean time (I know this behaviour exists). However, what I understand from the http protocol is that the browser would only be able to efficiently "stop" an http request as long as it's still on the browser side (establishing connection or some other state). Once the browser sent the request and server has received it and started processing it, the browser cannot do anything about it anymore, even if there _is_ a second one leaving from the browser, it can no longer stop the first one.

So I would say that the result of such an experiment can heavily depend on the timing of the clicks. Re-clicking regularly very fast could endup in the request / navigation being systematically re-initialized before being sent to the server. Maybe you need to give it a half a second or so to be able to start, and then click again. I enabled throttling on my browser to make the navigation slower to be able to play around with multiple clicks...

label: Fixed
summary: PDF Export Options modal keeps loading after restarting the remote headless Chrome
description:
When the PDF export is performed server-side using a headless Chrome, inside a Docker container or not, opening the PDF Export Modal after a Chrome restart can lead to an infinite loading. This has been noticed in our automated functional tests, when both XWiki (the servlet engine) and Chrome run inside a Docker container. But I'm pretty sure this can happen in other setups too.

The root problem is that the library we rely on to talk with the remote headless Chrome (https://github.com/kklisura/chrome-devtools-java-client) is using Java's {{HttpURLConnection}} to make the HTTP requests *without setting any timeout*. This means the HTTP requests we make to the remote headless Chrome can hang indefinitely or for a very long time.

Note that we tried setting (in various ways) {{sun.net.client.defaultConnectTimeout}} and {{sun.net.client.defaultReadTimeout}} as per https://bluxte.net/musings/2008/08/25/dont-forget-set-javaneturl-default-timeouts/ but it didn't help. In the end we think the best is to make these HTTP requests in a separate thread using an {{ExecutorService}} and to use a timeout when retrieving the {{Future}} results.

comments.author: Michael Hamann
comments.body:
The issue is on the client-side with the code for restoring the selection and in particular the diff computation that is used for it. Here a screenshot of the profiler:

 !firefox-profile.png|thumbnail!

comments.author: Michael Hamann
comments.body:
In the code, the slow diff call is here: https://github.com/xwiki/xwiki-platform/blob/6bbb277528374f801a3c256fd281234db844d9bb/xwiki-platform-core/xwiki-platform-ckeditor/xwiki-platform-ckeditor-plugins/src/main/webjar/xwiki-selection/plugin.js#L272

The diff method is from {{node-module!fast-diff}}. We're currently on version 1.2.0 of fast-diff but version 1.3.0 is available according to https://www.npmjs.com/package/fast-diff - according to https://github.com/jhchen/fast-diff/commits/master this version seems to have some fixes but nothing fundamental.

The used diff algorithm is fast if the number of differences is small but it becomes slow when there are many differences (quadratic in the worst case). I suspect that this is the problem here, possibly because of the huge number of links. The thing is that in our case we don't need the full diff so I'm wondering if we could avoid computing the full diff. Alternatively, we could in theory do the whole selection restoring without diff computation by keeping track of input positions in XWiki rendering. What I mean by this is that the parser would keep track of the selection position in the XDOM and when rendering to XWiki syntax we could compute the position of the selection in the output. But anyways, that's unfortunately just theory.

I can check if I can find anything regarding partial diffs, if you have any other realistic ideas, let me know.

comments.author: Marius Dumitru Florea
comments.body:
The diff is performed between the text content extracted from the DOM (CKEditor) and the wiki syntax (Source content). I attached the two files for testing:

*  [^diff-textContent.txt]
*  [^diff-wikiSyntax.txt]

I tried the 1.3.0 version of fast-diff, no change. I checked a bit the JavaScript code, especially the {{diff_bisect_}} function that takes most of the time, but I didn't see anything that can be improved. As [~MichaelHamann] said, we're simply hitting the limits of the diff algorithm due to a combination between large content and lots of differences between the text content and the wiki syntax. There are indeed many links which contribute to the large number of changes (16k if I recall correctly).

I tried another diff library https://www.npmjs.com/package/diff, but the results were worse. I also tried doing a *word* diff (fast-diff supports only char-level diff) but it didn't help. Performing a word diff should normally lead to fewer changes, I think, but it's more expensive to compare words (than characters) so in the end it takes longer.

I also tried using a *context* around the text selection (caret) to reduce the text that is being compared. A context of 1k characters reduces the time considerably, to less than 1s (which I find acceptable for the size of the document), but the restored selection / caret is often not in the right place. So I don't see how a partial diff as [~MichaelHamann] suggested can work. The fact is that you can have:

* *a lot*

comments.author: Marius Dumitru Florea
Michael Hamann
comments.body:
bq. I'm reading https://ably.com/blog/practical-guide-to-diff-algorithms . It seems there are some better algorithms (although the format of the produced patch is different, so it may require a refactoring of the selection restore code), but not many implementations.

I also read this article but the "better" algorithms don't produce a diff, they just produce a compact patch that wouldn't help in our case at all from what I understand. For example, if the diff inserts "[[" repeatedly, it would just copy that sequence several times instead of inserting it several times. Or it could copy whole blocks of text. I cannot see how we could determine the cursor position from this.

I had a look at git diff and its output seems quite sub-optimal but I haven't checked if the other diff implementations were better. But maybe it is using some tricks to be faster at the cost of reduced quality? Alternatively, it could also just be the advantage of a well-tuned implementation in C.

comments.author: Michael Hamann
comments.body: While comparing the running time of our Java diff implementation to a diff implementation used in IntelliJ I noticed that for a diff that didn't finish within hours with our Java implementation, IntelliJ produced a diff within seconds. Profiling the Java diff implementation showed that it spends basically all running time allocating tiny objects. Remembering what I learned and experienced about implementation differences I thought that maybe there is a faster implementations of the same diff algorithm. I started looking for performance benchmarks and found [https://github.com/gliese1337/fast-myers-diff] which is a JavaScript implementation of Myers diff algorithm that claims to be about 50x faster than fast-diff (the library we're currently using) in some of the tested cases. I think it would be worth testing it and seeing if this reduces the running time enough to not to be an issue anymore.

comments.author: Marius Dumitru Florea
comments.body:
The first problem is caused by the fact that *standalone* images are rendered inside a paragraph which is not floating as the image. We basically get: {noformat}

text before

<--- doesn't float, so it has 0 height <--- floats left or right

text after

{noformat} When PagedJS splits the content into print pages it checks if the paragraph that wraps the image fits the current print page and it always does.. because its height is 0. The floating image has left the wrapping paragraph "without content" (because the image is the only content). I tried to apply the same float style to the wrapping paragraph before PagedJS perform the print layout. This improves the result a bit: the text is not cut anymore but the image still is. The floating paragraph now has a proper height so PagedJS detects that there is an overflow but unfortunately it doesn't find the right split / overflow point. The bug seems to be in [{{findOverflow}}|https://gitlab.coko.foundation/pagedjs/pagedjs/-/blob/v0.4.3/src/chunker/layout.js#L626]. Basically PagedJS thinks that a floating image never overflows the print page... so instead of splitting the content before the image it continues to search for the overflow after the image. Fixing this is tricky because the {{!isFloat}} check is pretty old (more than 5 years old) and I suppose it was added for a reson. I'm afraid that dorping this, even just for images, will lead to side effects. An easy workaround is to re

label: Fixed
summary: Email notifications are sent at each restart of the server if a Bcc address is configured in Administration
description:
*Steps to reproduce*
 # Edit {{xwiki.properties}} and set {{notifications.emails.live.graceTime = 1}} to enable the sending of e-mails after 1 minute
 # Login as Admin
 # Go to Administer Wiki > Mail > Mail Sending
 # Configure email sending settings _including a BCC email address_
 # Optional: set "Discard Success Statuses" to No
 # Login as an user (e.g. U1) which has an email address set in his profile
 # Click on Notifications Bell and set all Watch toggles to ON (make sure on Notifications Settings > Applications section the Pages toggles are set to ON for Email column)
 # Set "Email Frequency" to Live
 # Login as Admin or other user
 # Create a page
 # Wait (app 1 min) and confirm that the email notification for the page creation event is received by the user
 # Close and restart the XWiki instance
 # After restart, observe the user's email inbox

*Expected results*

No email is received, since the email notification for page creation event was received already before the restart of the instance.

*Actual results*

The email notification is received again.

In Administration > Mail > Mail Sending Status, after every instance restart, the respective mail job sent is listed with the Status "send_success".

Reproduced also on XWiki 15.5.1.

label: Fixed
summary: XSS/CSRF RCE in XWiki.ConfigurableClass
description:
*Steps to reproduce:*

As an admin user, open {{<xwiki-host>/xwiki/bin/view/%22%3E%7B%7B%2Fhtml%7D%7D%7B%7Basync%20context%3D%22request/parameters%22%7D%7D%7B%7Bvelocity%7D%7D%23evaluate(%24request/eval)/?sheet=XWiki.ConfigurableClass&xpage=view&eval=$services.logging.getLogger(%22attacker%22).error(%22Attack%20success%20$hasProgramming%22)}} where {{<xwiki-host>}} is the URL of your XWiki installation.

Alternatively, as a user with edit right, first create a configurable section as, e.g., explained on XWIKI-21121.

*Expected result:*

The code in the URL is not executed.

*Actual result:*

A message like

{noformat}
2023-07-25 17:24:07,226 [org.xwiki.rendering.async.internal.AsyncRendererJob@778eca14([async, macro, xwiki:XWiki.ConfigurableClass, 8, author, xwiki:XWiki.Admin, rendering.restricted, false, request.parameters, {xpage=[Ljava.lang.String;@6d34dae1, sheet=[Ljava.lang.String;@7a1c53cf, eval=[Ljava.lang.String;@43bfe9cb}, secureDocument, xwiki:XWiki.ConfigurableClass, 459])] ERROR attacker                       - Attack success true 
{noformat}

is logged, showing that that code has been executed with programming right.

For this attack to succeed, the user needs to have edit right on at least one configurable section so this is not a remote code execution attack from guest. However, it is possible to trick an admin into visiting the URL to trigger the attack, e.g., by embedding the URL as an image in a comment.

Also, via the same attack vector, XSS is possible, too.

It seems that the vulnerable code has been introduced in XAADMINISTRATION-112 which seems to have been released in XWiki 2.3, see https://www.xwiki.org/xwiki/bin/view/ReleaseNotes/ReleaseNotesXWikiEnterprise23#HEasierdevelopmentofconfigurableapplicationsusingXWiki.ConfigurableClass
